A puzzled friendly cartoon developer holds a key that fits only one box while the other three sit unopened, one slightly cracked open revealing it is missing a puzzle piece. specs.alt: A confused cartoon developer faces four similar delivery boxes that all share one identical door knocker, holding a key that fits only one box while a half-open box is missing a puzzle piece, illustrating how the four OpenCV PyPI wheels all import as cv2 yet only one ships the function you need.
specs.caption: Four OpenCV wheels knock on the same cv2 door, but only the one you actually installed has the function you are calling; the rest answer with an AttributeError.

specs.anchorText: an L2 matcher on binary descriptors compiles, runs, and produces nonsense matches
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: two friendly cartoon characters trying to plug mismatched connectors together. One character is made of smooth rounded float-like shapes holding a round plug; the other is made of blocky binary on-off light switches holding a square plug; the round plug and square socket clearly do not fit, yet a spark suggests it forces a connection anyway and produces a confused tangle of wrong-colored wires. Gentle humor, soft pastel palette, expressive faces, minimal clutter, generous margins. No text or lettering in the image. One clear metaphor: wrong distance norm for the descriptor type.
specs.alt: Two cartoon characters force a round float-shaped plug into a square binary-shaped socket; it sparks and produces a tangle of wrong wires, illustrating how pairing the L2 norm with binary descriptors, or Hamming with float descriptors, runs without error yet yields nonsense matches.
specs.caption: Match the distance to the descriptor: float descriptors want L2, binary descriptors want Hamming, and the wrong pairing runs happily while quietly producing garbage matches.

specs.anchorText: incremental versus global. Incremental SfM (COLMAP) starts from a good two-view pair and adds one image at a time
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a split-scene comparison of two friendly cartoon builders assembling the same small house from a pile of photos. On the left, a builder places one brick at a time and after every single brick walks all the way around to re-check the whole house, looking tired with a clock showing lots of time passed. On the right, a builder lays out all the bricks at once into position and checks the whole house a single time, looking relaxed with a clock showing little time. Gentle humor, soft palette, expressive characters, clear left-right contrast, generous margins. No text or lettering in the image. One clear metaphor: incremental one-at-a-time versus global all-at-once reconstruction.
specs.alt: A split cartoon shows two builders making the same house from photos: the left builder adds one brick then re-checks the entire house each time and looks exhausted by a long clock, the right builder places all bricks at once and checks just once with a short clock, illustrating incremental versus global structure-from-motion.
specs.caption: Incremental SfM re-checks the whole reconstruction after every image and pays the bundle-adjustment bill once per photo; global SfM solves everything at once and pays it once per dataset.

specs.anchorText: COLMAP returned two disconnected reconstructions, the front face and the back face
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a cartoon stone archway that has come apart into two separate floating halves with a visible gap between them, because the cartoon photographer circling it took pictures only of the front and only of the back with no overlapping views bridging the two. Tiny dotted camera icons orbit each half but none span the gap. A friendly puzzled photographer looks at the floating halves. Gentle humor, soft palette, expressive character, minimal clutter, generous margins. No text or lettering in the image. One clear metaphor: missing overlapping views split a reconstruction in two.
specs.alt: A cartoon stone archway floats as two separated halves with a gap between them while a puzzled photographer's camera icons orbit each half but none bridge the gap, illustrating how a lack of overlapping views causes structure-from-motion to return two disconnected reconstructions.
specs.caption: Structure-from-motion can only connect what shares features; capture the front and back of an object with no overlapping views and the reconstruction honestly splits in two.

specs.anchorText: the most common evaluation error in SLAM
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a friendly cartoon robot proudly holding up a tiny toy-sized path that a helpful but sneaky benchmark referee has secretly stretched on an elastic band to perfectly overlay a large ground-truth path, earning a glowing high score on a scoreboard. Beside it, the same little robot stands in a real warehouse where the path stays tiny and clearly does not reach the goal, looking dismayed, because there is no referee to stretch it. Gentle humor, soft pastel palette, expressive characters, clear two-panel contrast, generous margins. No text or lettering in the image. One clear metaphor: scale correction flatters a number on the benchmark but fails in the field.
specs.alt: A cartoon robot earns a high benchmark score because a referee secretly stretches its tiny estimated path to match the true path, but in a real warehouse with no referee the same undersized path falls short of the goal, illustrating how monocular scale correction flatters a trajectory metric that fails in deployment.
specs.caption: A monocular trajectory looks excellent only because the benchmark quietly rescales it to match ground truth; on the warehouse floor there is no referee to stretch the path, and the hidden scale error reappears.

specs.anchorText: the network forgets, the geometry does not
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background: a wise, friendly old hardback reference book with a worn green spine and a kind face, calmly pointing a reading lamp at a sleek modern cartoon neural-network robot that has a puzzled tangle above its head over a slightly crooked geometric shape. The old book gently shows the robot the correct straight geometry, like a patient mentor. Soft palette, gentle humor, expressive characters, minimal clutter, generous margins. No text or lettering in the image. One clear metaphor: the classical geometry textbook diagnoses the learned method's failure.
specs.alt: A friendly worn green hardback textbook with a kind face shines a lamp to help a puzzled modern neural-network robot fix a crooked geometric shape, illustrating how the classical Hartley and Zisserman geometry reference remains the debugging manual for learned reconstruction methods that fail in the same geometric ways.
specs.caption: Learned methods still produce the same camera matrices and fail in the same geometric ways, so the patient old green book remains the fastest debugging tool: the network forgets, the geometry does not.
